results.answer: He built exact rate limiting on Durable Objects after measuring that the platform's built-in options let traffic through. results.question: What is AI Change Review?
results.answer: AI Change Review is a multi-agent Claude system Brett built end to end at Applied Systems that risk-checks every change before people approve it. It gathers evidence from the change ticket and its linked documents, freezes a snapshot, masks personal information, then runs six specialist agents with six validators and a final agent that writes one page of risks and concerns onto the ticket. It went from concept to production in under three months, was approved by Legal and InfoSec, and is used by five change advisory boards, with 1,900+ reviews across about 1,000 changes at roughly 10 minutes each. The key design choice: deterministic rules decide the risk tier, the AI is advisory only, and people make every decision.

results.question: How long did AI Change Review take to reach production?
results.answer: Under three months from concept to production. Brett built it end to end, and it went live with Legal and InfoSec approval — both teams commended how thorough his documentation and security practices were, without being asked. It's now used by five change advisory boards, with 1,900+ reviews across roughly 1,000 changes at about 10 minutes each.

results.question: How did he get an AI system approved by Legal and InfoSec?
results.answer: He got it approved by designing it so the AI never holds the decision. Deterministic, re-runnable rules decide the risk tier, the six specialist agents are advisory only, and people still make every approval; personal information is masked before anything reaches the model, and there are model kill switches and a full audit trail. He also replayed real past changes through the rules to show exactly where they would be right or wrong, and documented it thoroughly enough that Legal and InfoSec commended his documentation and security practices without being asked. The result was concept to production in under three months, now used by five change advisory boards.

results.question: What is Shepherd?
results.answer: Shepherd is Brett's own production AI platform for e-bike repair shops, built on Cloudflare and used by real shop staff since April 2025. It pairs a Claude-based repair agent with a 126,714-part catalog from 82 vendor sources, four production MCP servers behind OAuth, and evaluation gates on every AI change. It started as the system for his own shop and stays a side project and proof of work; it took 3rd Place and People's Choice at OPO Startups Demo Day 2025. Happy to go deeper on the AI and retrieval side or the reliability work.

results.question: How many MCP servers has he built?
results.answer: Brett has built four production MCP servers on Cloudflare, with 113 tools between them, all behind OAuth: one for Microsoft 365, Outlook.com and Gmail, one for RingCentral, one for Shepherd itself, and one for marketing data. He also built the OAuth 2.1 MCP endpoint in his open-source EdgeFetch project, and he helped define MCP governance for his company's enterprise AI program. Want me to go deeper on any one of them?

results.question: Tell me about the reranker he removed.
results.answer: Brett removed a reranker from Shepherd's search after measuring that it was consuming 60 to 85 percent of search latency while making accuracy worse. Taking it out dropped median search time from 1,073 ms to 342 ms and improved results. It's a good example of his rule that every retrieval or ranking change has to pass evaluation suites before release, and that a "smarter" component gets cut when the numbers say it hurts. He applied the same discipline to vendor models, rejecting three whose benchmark claims didn't hold on his own data.

results.question: How does he make sure an AI change is actually better?
results.answer: He gates every AI change behind evaluation suites built from his own real data, and nothing ships until it beats the current version on those numbers. That discipline has raised diagnostic top-1 accuracy from 16/20 to 19–20/20, and it also made him remove a reranker that measured slower and less accurate, cutting median search from 1,073 ms to 342 ms. He has rejected three vendor models whose benchmark claims didn't hold on his data, including one advertised as 10× faster that measured slower and ranked a trap answer above the correct one. He also writes the 500-case retrieval suite from the source documents rather than from search results, so the tests can't just agree with the system they're checking.

results.question: Does he know Kubernetes?
results.answer: Yes. Brett built two greenfield AKS clusters as code, using CNI Overlay, Cilium, Workload Identity and Entra ID with Azure RBAC, and he owns delivery for 30+ environments across Azure, on-premises and GCP. He also right-sized a 50-node Selenium grid, cutting compute about 40% with zero OOMKills at peak, and designed Kubernetes-based CI scaling about 45% cheaper than adding VMs from 30 days of real build data. He attended KubeCon NA 2026 and wrote a four-part series comparing agent state on Kubernetes and on the edge.

results.question: Tell me about the rate limiter he built on Durable Objects.
results.answer: He built exact rate limiting on Durable Objects after measuring that the platform's built-in options let traffic through: at a limit of 30, a burst of 45 requests admitted 44 with KV and the native limiter, while the Durable Object admitted exactly 30. He then added a sliding window that cut boundary overshoot from 27% to 3%. It's part of Shepherd's reliability work, where he tests the safety net by showing it fail on the bad case first. Happy to go deeper on the sliding-window design if useful.

results.question: What is AI Change Review?
results.answer: AI Change Review is a multi-agent Claude system Brett built end to end at Applied Systems that risk-checks every change before people approve it. It gathers evidence from the ticket and its linked documents into a frozen snapshot, masks personal information, then has six specialist agents review the change with six validators checking their work against that evidence, ending in a one-page summary of risks linked on the ticket. Deterministic rules decide the risk tier while the AI stays advisory, so people make every decision. It went from concept to production in under three months, was approved by Legal and InfoSec, and is used by five change advisory boards with 1,900+ reviews across about 1,000 changes at roughly 10 minutes each.

results.question: How long did AI Change Review take to reach production?
results.answer: Under three months from concept to production. Brett built it end to end, and it went live with Legal and InfoSec approval — both teams commended how thorough his documentation and security practices were, without being asked. It's now used by five change advisory boards, with 1,900+ reviews across roughly 1,000 changes at about 10 minutes each.

results.question: How did he get an AI system approved by Legal and InfoSec?
results.answer: He made the AI advisory, not authoritative. Deterministic, re-runnable rules decide the risk tier and people make every decision, while the six specialist agents only surface risks and concerns. He masked personal information before anything reached the model, added model kill switches and a full audit trail, and replayed real past changes through the rules to show exactly where they'd be right or wrong. It went from concept to production in under three months, and Legal and InfoSec both commended how thorough his documentation and security practices were, without being asked.

results.question: Tell me about the reranker he removed.

Taking it out dropped median search time from 1,073 ms to 342 ms, and results got better, not worse. It's a good example of his rule that every retrieval change has to pass evaluation suites before release, and that a "smarter" component gets cut when the numbers say it isn't helping. He later rejected a newer reranker too, after it dropped chat top-1 from 15/21 to 13/21 on two identical runs.

results.question: How does he make sure an AI change is actually better?
results.answer: He gates every AI change behind an evaluation harness he builds first, so a change ships only if it measurably wins. On Shepherd that discipline raised diagnostic top-1 accuracy from 16/20 to 19–20/20, and it also made him remove a reranker that was 60–85% of search latency and made accuracy worse, cutting median search from 1,073 ms to 342 ms. He has rejected three vendor models whose benchmark claims didn't hold on his own data, including one advertised as 10× faster that measured slower and ranked a trap answer above the correct one. He also writes the conclusion next to the flag, so the next engineer knows what was already tried and why it failed.
